newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Former governor says he did not give away HK - paper.
newsitem.headline: Former governor says he did not give away HK - paper.

text.p: Former Hong Kong governor Lord Murray MacLehose has denied he pushed the issue of the colony's return to China during a 1979 meeting with late Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping.

MacLehose, who was governor from 1971 to 1982, told the English-language South China Morning Post in an interview in its Saturday edition he did not encourage China to take a tough stance over the end of Hong Kong's rural New Territories lease.
A number of authors have claimed that MacLehose, by unexpectedly raising the issue of the territory's handover at the meeting, forced Beijing's hand over Hong Kong's reversion.
"The funny thing was that it wasn't me who mentioned (it) first, it was Deng Xiaoping," he said.
"It is nonsense to think it was something you could just ignore. It had to be raised some time, I was going to raise it."
Deng had not been told the subject would be discussed.

China ceded Hong Kong Island and the Kowloon peninsula to Britain in 1842 and 1860 after going to war over the opium trade. In 1898, Beijing also leased the New Territories and outlying 235 islands to Britain for 99 years, an agreement that expires this July 1.

After the MacLehose visit in April 1979, then British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher visited the Chinese capital in September 1982, where Deng refused London's request for continued British administration of Hong Kong after 1997.

In 1983, Britain and China began negotiations on Hong Kong's future. A year later Thatcher and China's then Premier Zhao Ziyang signed an agreement requiring London to transfer sovereignty of the colony to China at midnight on June 30, 1997.
China has promised the territory of 6.4 million people that they can keep their economic and political way of life for 50 years after the July 1 handover.
